title: Book 1, Chapter 3 — Congress of the Peloponnesian Confederacy at Lacedaemon
paragraphs: The Athenians and Peloponnesians had the following grievances against each other before war broke out. Corinth's complaint was that her colony Potidæa, with Corinthian and Peloponnesian citizens inside it, was under siege. Athens, for her part, complained that the Peloponnesians had incited a town of hers — a member of her alliance and a contributor to her revenue — to revolt, and had openly come and fought against her on the side of the Potidæans. Even so, the war had not yet broken out: there was still a truce in force, since this had been a private undertaking on Corinth's part.

But the siege of Potidæa put an end to her inaction. She had her own men inside the city, and she also feared for the place itself. She immediately summoned the allies to Lacedaemon, and once there she loudly accused Athens of breaking the treaty and violating the rights of the Peloponnese. The Aeginetans came with her. Formally they sent no representatives, out of fear of Athens, but in private they were among the most insistent advocates for war, claiming that Athens had denied them the independence the treaty guaranteed. The Lacedaemonians extended the summons to any of their allies and others who had complaints to make about Athenian aggression. Then they held their ordinary assembly and invited the speakers to come forward. Many came forward and made their various accusations. The Megarians, in a long list of grievances, drew special attention to the fact that they had been excluded from the ports of the Athenian empire and from the market of Athens, in defiance of the treaty. The Corinthians came forward last. They had let the previous speakers inflame the Lacedaemonians, and now they followed up with a speech to this effect:

"Lacedaemonians! The confidence you feel in your own constitution and social order makes you receive any criticism we offer about other powers with a certain skepticism. This is the source of your moderation, but also of the rather limited grasp of foreign politics that you display. Time and again we raised our voice to warn you of the blows Athens was about to deal us, and time and again, instead of taking the trouble to find out whether what we said was true, you contented yourselves with suspecting that the speakers were driven by private interest. So instead of calling these allies together before the blow fell, you have delayed until we are smarting under it — allies who are not the worst-qualified to speak, since we have the greatest grievances to bring: complaints of Athenian outrage and Lacedaemonian neglect. Now, if these attacks on the rights of Hellas had been made in secret, you might be ignorant of the facts, and our duty would be to inform you. But as it is, long speeches are not needed where you can see for yourselves that some of us have already been enslaved, that the same fate is being prepared for others — particularly our allies — and that the aggressor has long been preparing for the hour of war. Otherwise what is the meaning of their fraudulent reception of Corcyra, and their holding it against us by force? What is the meaning of the siege of Potidæa? — one of which lies most conveniently for any campaign against the Thracian towns, while the other would have contributed a very large fleet to the Peloponnesians.

"For all of this you are responsible. You were the ones who first allowed them to fortify their city after the Median war, and afterwards to build the long walls — you who, then and now, are constantly stripping freedom not only from those they have already enslaved, but also from those who have been your own allies up till now. The true author of a people's subjugation is not so much the one who carries it out, but the power that has the means to prevent it and does not — particularly if that power claims the glory of being the liberator of Hellas. We have at last assembled. It has not been easy to assemble, and even now our objectives are not clearly defined. We ought no longer to be inquiring into the fact that we have been wronged, but into the means of our defence. The aggressors have laid mature plans against our indecision, and have cast aside threats and turned to action. We know the paths along which Athenian aggression travels, and how insidious its progress is. She may take some confidence from the idea that your bluntness of perception keeps you from noticing her, but that is nothing compared to the impulse her advance will gain from learning that you see what she is doing and yet do not care to interfere. You Lacedaemonians, alone among the Hellenes, are inactive, and you defend yourselves not by doing anything but by looking as though you might. You alone wait until an enemy's power has doubled, instead of crushing it in its infancy. The world used to say you could be relied on, but in your case, we fear, that was more than the truth. The Mede, as we ourselves know, had time to come from the ends of the earth to the Peloponnese without any force of yours worth the name advancing to meet him. But that was a distant enemy. Athens, at any rate, is a near neighbor, and yet you utterly disregard her. Against Athens you prefer to act on the defensive rather than the offensive, and to leave matters to chance by putting off the struggle until she has grown far stronger than she was at the start. And yet you know that, on the whole, the rock the barbarian was wrecked on was himself, and that if Athens, our present enemy, has not destroyed us again and again, we owe it more to her own blunders than to any protection from you. Indeed, expectations from you have already ruined some who, trusting in your support, neglected their own preparations.

"We hope none of you will take these words of ours as words of hostility rather than remonstrance. Men remonstrate with friends who are in error; accusations they reserve for enemies who have wronged them. Besides, we consider that we have as good a right as anyone to point out a neighbor's faults, particularly when we look at the great contrast between the two national characters — a contrast which, as far as we can tell, you have barely perceived, having never yet considered what sort of opponents you will face in the Athenians, how widely, how absolutely different from yourselves they are. The Athenians are addicted to innovation, and their plans are marked by swiftness in both conception and execution. You have a genius for keeping what you have, combined with a complete lack of invention, and when you are forced to act you never go far enough. They are adventurous beyond their power, daring beyond their judgment, and confident in danger. Your habit is to attempt less than your power justifies, to mistrust even what your own judgment endorses, and to imagine that there is no escape from danger. There is promptness on their side against your delay. They are never at home; you are never away from it. They hope to extend their possessions by being absent; you fear that by advancing you will endanger what you have already secured. They are quick to follow up a success and slow to retreat from a setback. They spend their bodies ungrudgingly in their country's cause, and they jealously husband their intellect to be employed in her service. A scheme not yet carried out is, for them, a positive loss; a successful enterprise is a comparative failure. The gap created by a failed undertaking is quickly filled with fresh hopes — for they alone are able to call something hoped for already won, by the speed with which they act on their decisions. Thus they toil through trouble and danger all the days of their lives, with little chance to enjoy what they have, since they are always busy getting more. Their only idea of a holiday is to do whatever the moment demands, and to them strenuous activity is less of a misfortune than the peace of a quiet life. To put their character in a single word, one might truthfully say that they were born into the world to take no rest themselves and to give none to others.

"Such is Athens, your antagonist. And yet, Lacedaemonians, you still delay, and fail to see that peace lasts longest for those who are no less careful to use their power justly than to make it clear they will not submit to injustice. On the contrary, your idea of fair dealing rests on the principle that, if you do not injure others, you need not put your own fortunes at risk to keep others from injuring you. You could hardly have succeeded in such a policy even with a neighbor like yourselves, and in the present case, as we have just shown, your habits are old-fashioned compared to theirs. The law in politics, as in art, is that improvements always prevail. Fixed customs may be best for undisturbed communities, but the constant demand for action must be met with constantly improved methods. That is how Athens, with her vast experience, has gone further than you down the path of innovation.

"Here at least let your delay end. For the present, help your allies — and Potidæa in particular, as you promised — by a quick invasion of Attica. Do not sacrifice friends and kinsmen to their bitterest enemies, and do not drive the rest of us in despair to seek some other alliance. Such a step would not be condemned either by the gods who received our oaths or by the men who witnessed them. The breach of a treaty cannot be charged against the people whom desertion forces to seek new ties, but against the power that fails to support its confederate. But if you will only act, we will stand by you. It would be unnatural for us to change, and we would never find such a congenial ally. So choose the right course, and try to keep the Peloponnese, under your supremacy, from sinking below the standing it enjoyed under your ancestors."

Such was the speech of the Corinthians. There happened to be Athenian envoys at Lacedaemon at the time on other business. On hearing the speeches they thought they should come forward before the Lacedaemonians. Their intention was not to defend themselves against any of the charges the cities brought against them, but to argue, on a broader view, that the matter was not one to be hastily decided, but demanded further reflection. They also wanted to call attention to Athens' great power, to refresh the memory of the older men and inform the younger ones, in the hope that their words might persuade the Lacedaemonians to prefer peace to war. So they came to the Lacedaemonians and said that they too, if there was no objection, wished to address the assembly. The Lacedaemonians invited them to come forward. The Athenians advanced and spoke as follows:

"The purpose of our mission here was not to argue with your allies, but to handle the business our state sent us on. However, the violence of the outcry against us has persuaded us to come forward — not to answer the charges of the cities (indeed, you are not the judges before whom either we or they could plead), but to keep you from taking the wrong course in matters of great importance by yielding too easily to the persuasions of your allies. We also want to show, in a review of the whole indictment, that we have a fair claim to what we possess, and that our country deserves consideration. We need not refer to the distant past: there we could appeal to tradition, but not to the experience of our audience. We must refer, though, to the Median War and to recent history, even if we are rather tired of bringing this subject up again and again. In our actions during that war, we ran great risks to obtain certain results. You shared in the solid benefits — do not try to rob us of any share in the glory those results may bring us. The story will be told not so much to deprecate hostilities as to bear witness against them, and to show, if you are foolish enough to enter into a struggle with Athens, what sort of opponent she is likely to prove. We assert that at Marathon we stood at the front and faced the barbarian alone. When he came the second time, unable to face him on land, we boarded our ships with all our people and joined the engagement at Salamis. This prevented him from picking off the Peloponnesian states one by one and ravaging them with his fleet, when the sheer number of his vessels would have made any combined defence impossible. The clearest proof of this came from the invader himself. Defeated at sea, he judged that his power was no longer what it had been, and withdrew as quickly as possible with the larger part of his army.

"Such, then, was the outcome, and it was clearly proved that the cause of Hellas hung on her fleet. To that result we contributed three very useful elements: the largest number of ships, the ablest commander, and the most unhesitating patriotism. Our contingent was little less than two-thirds of the whole four hundred ships. The commander was Themistocles, who was chiefly responsible for fighting the battle in the straits — which everyone agrees was the salvation of our cause. That, indeed, was why you welcomed him with honors such as had never been given to any foreign visitor. As for daring patriotism, we had no rivals. Receiving no reinforcements from behind, seeing everything in front of us already subdued, we still had the spirit, after abandoning our city and sacrificing our property — rather than deserting the rest of the league or depriving them of our help by scattering — to throw ourselves into our ships and face the danger, without resenting your failure to come to our aid. We claim, therefore, that we gave you quite as much as we received. You had a stake to fight for: the cities you had left behind were still standing with your homes intact, and you had the prospect of enjoying them again. Your coming was driven as much by fear for yourselves as by concern for us — and you never appeared until we had nothing left to lose. But we left behind a city that was no longer a city, and staked our lives for one that existed only in desperate hope. So we bore our full share in your deliverance as well as our own. If we had imitated others and let fear for our territory drive us into siding with the Mede before you arrived, or if we had let our ruin break our spirit and stop us from boarding our ships, your naval inferiority would have made a sea-battle pointless, and the Mede would have achieved his aims peacefully.

"Surely, Lacedaemonians, neither the patriotism we showed in that crisis nor the wisdom of our counsel earns us such extreme unpopularity with the Hellenes — at least, not unpopularity for our empire. That empire we did not acquire by violence: we acquired it because you were unwilling to see the war against the barbarian through to its end, and because the allies attached themselves to us and spontaneously asked us to take the command. The nature of the case then forced us to bring the empire to its present height, with fear as our principal motive, though honor and interest came in afterwards. At last, when nearly everyone hated us, when some had already revolted and been brought back, when you had ceased to be the friends you once were and had become objects of suspicion and dislike, it no longer seemed safe to give up our empire — especially since all who left us would fall to you. No one can quarrel with a people for making, in matters of enormous risk, the best provision it can for its own interests.

"You, at any rate, Lacedaemonians, have used your supremacy to arrange the states of the Peloponnese to suit yourselves. And if, at the period we were speaking of, you had persevered to the end and incurred hatred in your command, we are sure you would have made yourselves just as galling to the allies, and would have been forced to choose between a strong government and danger to yourselves. So it was no remarkable action on our part, or contrary to the common practice of mankind, if we accepted an empire offered to us and refused to give it up under the pressure of three of the strongest motives — fear, honor, and interest. We did not set the example: it has always been the rule that the weaker should be subject to the stronger. Besides, we believed we deserved our position, and you thought so too, until calculations of interest made you take up the cry of justice — a consideration no one has ever yet brought forward to obstruct his ambition when he had a chance of gaining anything by force. And praise is due to all who, even if they are not so superior to human nature as to refuse dominion, still respect justice more than their position requires them to.

"We imagine that the best demonstration of our moderation would be the conduct of others put in our position. But our fairness, very unreasonably, has earned us condemnation rather than approval. The fact that we hold our contract trials with our allies on equal terms, and have them decided by impartial laws at Athens, has gained us the reputation of being litigious. No one cares to ask why this reproach is not brought against other imperial powers who treat their subjects with less moderation than we do. The reason is that where force can be used, law is not needed. Our subjects, though, are so used to dealing with us as equals that any setback that clashes with their idea of justice — whether it comes from a legal verdict or from the power our empire gives us — makes them forget to be grateful that they are still allowed to keep most of their possessions. They are more vexed at losing a part than they would have been if we had cast law aside from the start and openly indulged our greed. If we had done that, even they would not have disputed that the weaker must give way to the stronger. Men's indignation, it seems, is more excited by a legal wrong than by a violent one: the first looks like being cheated by an equal, the second like being compelled by a superior. They certainly managed to put up with much worse treatment than this from the Mede, and yet they think our rule severe — which is to be expected, since the present always weighs heaviest on the conquered. This much at least is certain. If you were to succeed in overthrowing us and taking our place, you would quickly lose the popularity that fear of us has given you, supposing your present policy at all matches the sample you gave during the brief period of your command against the Mede. Not only is your life at home regulated by rules and institutions incompatible with those of others, but your citizens abroad act neither by these rules nor by those recognized by the rest of Hellas.

"Take your time, then, in forming your resolution, since the matter is of great importance. Do not let yourselves be persuaded by the opinions and complaints of others to bring trouble on yourselves. Consider the enormous influence of accident in war before you commit to it. As war drags on, it generally becomes a matter of chance — chance from which neither of us is exempt, and whose outcome we have to risk in the dark. It is a common mistake when going to war to start at the wrong end: to act first, and only discuss the matter once disaster has struck. But we are not yet so misguided, and as far as we can see, neither are you. So while it is still open to both of us to choose rightly, we ask you not to dissolve the treaty, or to break your oaths, but to settle our differences by arbitration as our agreement provides. Otherwise we call the gods who heard the oaths to witness that, if you begin hostilities, whatever course of action you choose, we will try not to be slow in repelling you."

Such were the words of the Athenians. After the Lacedaemonians had heard the complaints of the allies against the Athenians, and the response of the Athenians, they made everyone withdraw and consulted privately on the question before them. The opinions of the majority all pointed to the same conclusion: the Athenians were open aggressors, and war must be declared at once. But Archidamus, the Lacedaemonian king, who had the reputation of being both wise and moderate, came forward and made the following speech:

"I have not lived this long, Lacedaemonians, without experiencing many wars, and I see those of you who are my own age and will not fall into the common mistake of longing for war out of inexperience or out of a belief in its advantages and its safety. The war you are now debating would, on a sober view of the matter, be one of the greatest scale. In a struggle with Peloponnesians and neighbors our strength is of the same character as theirs, and we can move quickly to different points. But a struggle with a people who live in a distant land, who also have an extraordinary familiarity with the sea, and who are at the highest pitch of preparation in every other department too — with private and public wealth, with ships and horses and heavy infantry, with a population no other Hellenic place can match, and finally with a host of tributary allies — what justifies us in rashly beginning such a war? Where is our confidence that we should rush into it unprepared? Is it in our ships? There we are inferior, and if we are to practice and become a match for them, time will have to pass. Is it in our money? There our deficiency is far greater. We have nothing in our treasury, and we are not ready to contribute it from our private funds. We might place some confidence in our superiority in heavy infantry and population, which will allow us to invade and ravage their lands. But the Athenians have plenty of other land in their empire, and can import what they need by sea. Again, if we try to incite a revolt of their allies, those allies will need a fleet to support them, since most of them are islanders. What kind of war, then, is this to be? Unless we can either beat them at sea or strip them of the revenues that feed their navy, we will gain little but disaster. Meanwhile our honor will be committed to seeing the war through, especially if it comes to be thought that we started the quarrel. Let us never be carried away by the fatal hope that the war can be quickly ended by ravaging their land. I rather fear we may leave it as a legacy to our children — so unlikely is it that the Athenian spirit will be enslaved to its land, or Athenian experience cowed by war.

"Not that I would have you so unfeeling as to let them harm your allies and refrain from exposing their plots. But I urge you not to take up arms at once. Send and remonstrate with them in a tone neither too suggestive of war nor too suggestive of submission, and use the interval to perfect our own preparations. The means will be, first, the acquisition of allies — Hellenic or barbarian, it does not matter, as long as they add to our strength either in ships or in money. I say Hellenic or barbarian, because the odium of such an alliance is canceled, for all of us who like ourselves are targets of Athenian designs, by the law of self-preservation. Secondly, the development of our home resources. If they listen to our embassy, so much the better; if not, after two or three years our position will have been substantially strengthened, and we can then attack them if we think it best. Perhaps by then the sight of our preparations, backed by language equally clear, will have inclined them to submission, while their land is still untouched and their counsels can still aim at preserving advantages not yet destroyed. The only way you can view their land is as a hostage in your hands, and a hostage that is the more valuable the better cultivated it is. You ought to spare it as long as possible, rather than make them desperate and so make them harder to deal with. If we let ourselves be hurried by the complaints of our allies into laying it waste while we are still unprepared, beware that we do not bring deep disgrace and deep difficulty upon the Peloponnese. Complaints — whether of communities or individuals — can be settled. But a war undertaken by a coalition for sectional interests, whose course no one can foresee, does not lend itself easily to a creditable settlement.

"And no one need think it cowardice if a number of confederates pause before attacking a single city. The Athenians have as many allies as we do, and allies that pay tribute. War is not so much a matter of arms as of money, which makes arms of any use. This is truer than ever in a struggle between a land power and a sea power. So let us first provide money, and not let ourselves be swept along by the talk of our allies before we have done so. Since we will bear the largest share of the responsibility for the outcome, good or bad, we also have a right to deliberate calmly about it.

"The slowness and delay that our character is most criticized for need not make you blush. If we undertake the war without preparation, we will only delay its conclusion by hastening its beginning. Moreover, a free and famous city has been ours through all time. The quality they condemn is really nothing but wise moderation. Thanks to it, we alone do not grow insolent in success and give way less than others in misfortune. We are not carried away by the pleasure of being cheered on into risks our judgment condemns. Nor, when annoyed, are we any more convinced by attempts to exasperate us with accusations. We are both warlike and wise, and our sense of order is what makes us so. We are warlike because self-control contains honor as a chief element, and honor contains bravery. And we are wise because we are educated with too little learning to despise the laws, and with too strict a self-control to disobey them. We are brought up not to be too clever in useless matters — such as the knowledge that can give a plausible critique of an enemy's plans in theory but fails to attack them with equal success in practice. Instead we are taught to consider that our enemies' schemes are not unlike our own, and that the accidents of chance cannot be calculated. In practice we always base our preparations against an enemy on the assumption that his plans are sound. It is right to rest our hopes not on a belief in his blunders, but on the soundness of our own arrangements. Nor should we suppose that there is much difference between one man and another — only that the advantage lies with the man reared in the strictest school. These practices, then, that our ancestors have handed down to us, and by which we have always profited, must not be abandoned. We must not be hurried into deciding in the brief space of a single day a question that concerns many lives and fortunes and many cities, and in which honor is deeply involved. We must decide calmly. Our strength is what especially enables us to do this. As for the Athenians, send to them on the matter of Potidæa, send on the matter of the alleged wrongs of the allies — particularly since they are prepared with legal satisfaction. To proceed against one who offers arbitration, as against a wrongdoer, the law forbids. Meanwhile do not neglect preparation for war. This decision will be best for you, and most fearsome to your opponents."
Such were the words of Archidamus. Last came forward Sthenelaidas, one of the ephors for that year, who spoke to the Lacedaemonians as follows:

"The long speech of the Athenians I do not claim to understand. They said a great deal in praise of themselves, but nowhere denied that they are wronging our allies and the Peloponnese. And yet if they behaved well against the Mede then but badly toward us now, they deserve double punishment, for having ceased to be good and for having become bad. We, meanwhile, are the same now as we were then. If we are wise, we will not disregard the wrongs of our allies, or put off until tomorrow the duty of helping those who must suffer today. Others have plenty of money and ships and horses, but we have good allies whom we must not abandon to the Athenians, nor settle the matter by lawsuits and words — for it is anything but in word that we are being harmed. We must give instant and powerful help. And let no one tell us that it is proper for us to deliberate when we are being wronged. Long deliberation is more proper for those who are contemplating wronging others. Vote, then, Lacedaemonians, for war, as the honor of Sparta demands. Do not allow the further growth of Athens, do not betray our allies to ruin, but with the gods on our side let us advance against the aggressors."

With these words, as ephor, he himself put the question to the assembly of the Lacedaemonians. He said he could not tell which was the louder acclamation (their mode of decision is by acclamation, not by voting). In fact he wanted to make them declare their opinion openly and so increase their ardor for war. So he said: "All Lacedaemonians who think the treaty has been broken and that Athens is guilty, leave your seats and go there" — pointing to a certain place — "all who hold the opposite opinion, there." They stood up and divided, and those who held that the treaty had been broken were in a decided majority. They then summoned the allies and told them that in their opinion Athens had committed injustice, but that they wished to convene all the allies and put it to a vote, so that they might make war, if so decided, on a common resolution. Having thus gained their point, the delegates returned home at once. The Athenian envoys followed a little later, once they had finished the business of their mission. This decision of the assembly, judging that the treaty had been broken, was made in the fourteenth year of the thirty years' truce that had been entered into after the affair of Euboea.

The Lacedaemonians voted that the treaty had been broken and that war must be declared, not so much because they were persuaded by the arguments of the allies as because they feared the growth of Athenian power, seeing most of Hellas already subject to them.
